name: Mercantilism
summary: Mercantilism was the economic policy and writing of early modern Europe, c. 1500 to 1780, that aimed at a rich and powerful state. Governments protected home manufactures with tariffs, quotas and export bans, granted monopolies, built navies and held colonies, in the belief that a surplus of exports over imports, paid in gold and silver, raised national power. It was less a finished system than a literature of pamphlets on practical questions, and its writers differed on money, interest and population.
scope: The mercantilism of the 16th to 18th centuries as the scholarship on the term defines it (Magnusson, LaHaye): the policy of the mercantilist states and the publicists Britannica and Magnusson name, here read through Thomas Mun's England's Treasure by Forraign Trade (1664), Colbert's 1664 memorandum to Louis XIV and the principles Britannica lists. It excludes later economic nationalism and modern neomercantilism, which both entries treat as successors. Most of the test's statements concern questions the writers never addressed, so they stay null.

missingStatements.text: A country should aim to export more than it imports.
missingStatements.rationale: Mun says to sell more to strangers yearly than is consumed of theirs, so the surplus returns as treasure, and the aim is central across mercantilist writing.

notes: Themes searched: trade policy, tariffs and monopolies, colonies, money and capital movements, armed forces and war, population, the role of the state (in Mun, Colbert, Magnusson, LaHaye, Britannica and, read but not cited, Steuart's Inquiry). Government (elections, courts, federalism), society and culture, liberty and ecology are themes the mercantilist writers did not address, so those statements stay null and the uncertainty rule is expected to exclude this ideology. Mercantilism was not one doctrine; Magnusson and others reject treating it as a finished system, and Mun and the earlier bullionists differed on exporting money.
